name: Doorstep Canvassing
description: Free, slow, and genuinely effective. Nobody ever won a news cycle knocking on doors.
flavour: Four hours of doorsteps. Two dogs, one shouting match, and a man who wanted to discuss the bins for forty minutes.

name: Staged Photo Op
description: High impact with the credulous. Everyone else can smell the staging.
flavour: The candidate holds a locally-sourced vegetable at an unnatural angle for nine minutes.

name: Media Buy
description: Expensive, broad, shallow. Buys a little goodwill absolutely everywhere.
flavour: Thirty seconds of drone footage over the seafront and a voiceover that says the word 'future' four times.

name: Attack Ad
description: Choose an opponent. Their voters may come your way; the backlash is everybody's problem.
flavour: A grainy black-and-white photograph of the opponent, slowly zooming, set to a cello.

name: Debate Prep
description: Moves no polls today. Steadies the candidate and gets your own voters to actually turn up.
flavour: Six hours in a function room teaching a grown adult not to say the first thing they think.

name: Commission a Quick Poll
description: A small sample, a fast turnaround, and a margin of error you could drive a campaign bus through.
flavour: The pollster phones in the topline. They sound confident. Their methodology is three people outside the post office.

name: Commission a Constituency Poll
description: A proper local sample. Accurate enough to change your mind, not enough to sleep well.
flavour: The crosstabs arrive in a spreadsheet with 47 tabs and one cell labelled 'probably fine'. The headline number is probably fine.

name: Commission a Full-Sample Poll
description: A large, weighted sample with proper fieldwork. The best estimate money can buy; still an estimate.
flavour: The agency sends a leather-bound report. It contains 86 pages, two contradictory recommendations, and a chart that makes the candidate look electable.

name: The Inside Track
description: A quiet word with someone who owes you one. You stop guessing and start knowing.
flavour: A retired pollster who trusts you shares their reading of published turnout figures. No confidential records, just experience and a coffee you now owe them.

requires.label: Credibility 68 — people only tip off operators they respect

special.failureHeadline: Inside tip proves outside the mark
special.failureFlavour: Your trusted source misreads the figures. You have spent a favour and vouched for bad information; neither is easily forgotten.

name: Call In a Favour
description: Ask an investigative reporter to verify a rival's real conflicts of interest. Credible evidence, not an invented scandal.
flavour: The paper publishes the documents and gives the opponent ample room to explain. Their explanation needs considerably more room.

requires.label: Credibility 76 — a reporter must trust your word

special.failureHeadline: Promised expose fails the fact check
special.failureFlavour: The documents do not support your claim. Nothing is published, but the reporter remembers who wasted their time.

name: Stake Your Good Name
description: Persuade respected community figures to endorse a properly costed promise. Your reputation is the collateral.
flavour: A row of usually sceptical local voices backs the pledge. They make it very clear that they are trusting you, not the rosette.

requires.label: Credibility 85 — your word can carry a public endorsement

special.failureFlavour: The endorsers decide the promise is too optimistic. You vouched for it, and your good name is a little less good.

name: Throw a Dead Cat
description: You have a file. It is not strictly relevant. It is, however, extremely interesting.
flavour: By lunchtime nobody is discussing the hospital. By teatime a man you have never met is resigning live on the local news, and your candidate is asking you questions you would rather he did not.

requires.label: Ruthlessness 45 — this file only reaches people who would use it

special.failureHeadline: Diversion traced back to campaign office
special.failureFlavour: The irrelevant scandal is traced to your desk. Instead of distracting from the hospital, you have made the campaign the story.

name: Frame an Opponent
description: A fabricated criminal allegation. A monstrous gamble dressed up as a press release; getting caught could end your account.
flavour: The invented allegation dominates the headlines. Your opponent loses support while demanding a retraction. This is not a victory you can defend.

requires.label: Ruthlessness 65 — you are willing to ruin an innocent rival

special.failureFlavour: Independent scrutiny exposes the fabrication. The rival is cleared and your client suddenly cannot remember your surname.

name: Tamper With the Vote
description: Voter fraud. No euphemism makes it legitimate. Half of these attempts are caught, and even a friendly client may sacrifice you.
flavour: An illicit scheme appears to boost support. The apparent gain comes with no moral victory and a campaign office full of people who will deny knowing you.

requires.label: Ruthlessness 80 — democratic consent is no longer your concern

special.failureFlavour: The watchdog exposes the scheme before it can produce a gain. Voters are furious; the client reaches for a prepared statement about rogue consultants.

name: Write a Personal Cheque
description: Your own money into the campaign account. Technically declarable. Eventually.
flavour: You move fifteen thousand pounds of your own money and tell yourself it is an investment in the relationship. The treasurer does not ask, and you do not volunteer.

requires.label: £15,000 of your own money left to burn
